concepts.name: Kharaj (Land Revenue Tax): Nature, Rates, and Assessment Methods
key_dimensions: Distinction between Kharaj as a proportional share (1/3 to 1/2 of produce) vs. fixed assessment — and which sultans used which method
Difference between Kharaj (for non-Muslims on conquered land) and Ushr (tithe for Muslims) — UPSC trap on conflation of the two
Alauddin Khalji's fixed cash-based Kharaj reform vs. earlier in-kind collection — policy shift significance
Firuz Shah Tughlaq's reversal to more flexible rates — contrast with Alauddin's rigid system

concepts.name: Alauddin Khalji's Revenue Reforms: Measurement and Market Control Nexus
key_dimensions: Introduction of measurement (Masahat) of land as the basis for revenue assessment — departure from produce-sharing
Connection between low grain prices (market reforms) and fixed land revenue in cash — interdependence often missed
Role of Diwan-i-Mustakhraj (department for recovery of arrears) in enforcing revenue collection
Elimination of intermediary chiefs (Khuts, Muqaddams, Chaudharies) from revenue collection — social implications

concepts.name: Kharaj vs. Ushr vs. Zakat: Taxation of Muslims vs. Non-Muslims
key_dimensions: Kharaj levied on non-Muslim cultivators on conquered land; Ushr (1/10th) on Muslim-owned irrigated land — comparative rates
Zakat as a religious tax on Muslims vs. Kharaj as a state tax — nature (religious obligation vs. revenue instrument)
UPSC trap: Ushr rate varying — 1/20th on unirrigated land vs. 1/10th on irrigated land for Muslims
Whether Sultans consistently applied this distinction — evidence of pragmatic deviation under later Tughlaqs

concepts.name: Jizya: Imposition, Exemptions, and Administrative Evolution in the Sultanate
key_dimensions: Jizya as a poll tax on zimmis (non-Muslims) — distinct from Kharaj which was on land, not persons
Exemptions: women, children, old, disabled, monks — UPSC frequently tests who was exempt
Firuz Shah Tughlaq extending Jizya to Brahmins (previously exempt) — a notable policy shift
Whether Jizya was merged with land revenue or collected separately — administrative ambiguity under different sultans

concepts.name: Firuz Shah Tughlaq's Revenue Policy: Consolidation and Concessions
key_dimensions: Abolition of around 23 cesses (abwabs) and consolidation into four canonical taxes — Kharaj, Kham, Jizya, Zakat
Irrigation tax (Haq-i-Sharb) introduced — 1/10th of produce on canal-irrigated land, a novel revenue source
Revival of assignments (Iqta) as hereditary grants — weakening of central revenue control vs. Alauddin's model
Contrast with Alauddin: Firuz's policy as welfare-oriented but fiscally weakening — long-term vs. short-term tradeoff

concepts.name: Iqta System: Revenue Assignment Mechanism and Its Evolution
key_dimensions: Iqta as assignment of revenue of a territory to an officer (Muqti/Wali) in lieu of salary — not land grant in ownership
Distinction between Iqta (revenue right) and Jagir (Mughal term) — UPSC frequently conflates these
Balban's reforms: strict accounting of surplus Iqta revenue to be deposited with the centre — centralization attempt
Firuz Shah's making Iqtas hereditary — structural shift that decentralized fiscal control and weakened the Sultanate

concepts.name: Diwan-i-Wizarat and Central Revenue Administration
key_dimensions: Diwan-i-Wizarat as the apex revenue/finance ministry headed by the Wazir — functions and limitations
Sub-departments: Diwan-i-Ariz (military pay), Diwan-i-Insha (correspondence), Diwan-i-Risalat — overlap with revenue functions, a UPSC trap area
Diwan-i-Mustakhraj under Alauddin: specialized department for revenue arrears recovery — unique innovation
Weakness of central revenue control under Firuz Shah vs. its peak under Alauddin — institutional comparison

concepts.name: Kham (State Share in War Booty and Special Levies)
key_dimensions: Kham as 1/5th share of war booty claimed by the state — Quranic basis (Anfal principle)
Extension of Kham concept to mines, treasure troves, and salt — beyond war booty
Firuz Shah listing Kham as one of four legitimate taxes — canonical status under him
Distinction from Ghanima (general war booty distributed among soldiers) — often confused in questions

concepts.name: Abwabs (Illegal Cesses) and Their Socioeconomic Impact
key_dimensions: Abwabs as extra, unauthorized local cesses collected by Muqaddams, Khuts, and revenue officials — not sanctioned by central authority
Alauddin's attempt to abolish Abwabs and fix only Kharaj — partially successful, recurred under successors
Firuz Shah's formal abolition of 23 Abwabs — listed them explicitly, signifying their widespread prevalence
Peasant burden: Abwabs as regressive taxes falling hardest on subsistence farmers — social history angle

concepts.name: Role of Khuts, Muqaddams, and Chaudharies in Revenue Extraction
key_dimensions: Khuts (village headmen of higher status), Muqaddams (village headmen), Chaudharies (regional intermediaries) — hierarchy and distinction, a classic UPSC confusion point
Their dual role: intermediaries between state and peasants, but also exploiters extracting surplus via Abwabs
Alauddin's policy of taxing them equally as peasants and denying exemptions — radical equalizing measure
Firuz Shah's restoration of their privileges — reversal and its consequence for revenue efficiency

concepts.name: Alauddin Khalji's Market Reforms as a Revenue-Military Instrument
key_dimensions: Four markets (grain, cloth, cattle/horses, slaves/cattle) — purpose was to maintain a large army at low cost, not consumer welfare
Shahna-i-Mandi (market controller) and Barid (intelligence) as enforcement mechanisms — administrative innovation
Fixed prices enabling low cash salaries to soldiers — indirect revenue conservation mechanism, often missed in analysis
Failure after Alauddin's death: why the system was unsustainable — structural dependency on autocratic enforcement

concepts.name: Irrigation Infrastructure and Revenue: Firuz Shah's Canal System
key_dimensions: Firuz Shah constructing major canals (Yamuna-Hisar canal, Sutlej-Ghaggar canal) — largest pre-Mughal irrigation network
Haq-i-Sharb (water tax at 1/10th of produce) as a new revenue stream tied to canal irrigation
Relationship between agricultural expansion via irrigation and overall revenue base growth
Contrast with Alauddin who focused on revenue extraction from existing agriculture vs. Firuz's revenue expansion strategy

concepts.name: Token Currency Experiment of Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Fiscal Context
key_dimensions: Introduction of bronze/copper token currency (1330) as a response to treasury depletion from failed campaigns and extravagant grants
Failure due to lack of state capacity to prevent private minting — administrative, not just economic failure
Revenue implications: state accepted token currency for taxes but paid real silver for purchases — asymmetric fiscal drain
Lesson for UPSC: contrast with successful paper money in China (Marco Polo's account) — why it worked there but not here

concepts.name: Doab Policy of Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Revenue Enhancement Gone Wrong
key_dimensions: Increase in land revenue in the Doab (Ganga-Yamuna region) — between 10% to 100% increase (sources vary) — occurring simultaneously with a famine
Timing disaster: revenue hike during agricultural distress caused peasant flight and agrarian collapse
State response: agricultural loans (Taccavi/Sondhar) introduced to revive cultivation — positive policy innovation in isolation
Overall lesson: revenue maximization without agrarian stability is self-defeating — Barni's critique as a primary source angle

concepts.name: Taccavi (Agricultural Loans) as a State Revenue Instrument
key_dimensions: Taccavi as state loans to peasants for seeds, implements, and relief during famines — welfare and revenue-recovery tool combined
Muhammad bin Tughlaq's large-scale Taccavi in the Doab as early state intervention in agriculture
Distinction from modern agricultural credit: Taccavi was interest-free or low-interest — not purely commercial
Firuz Shah also used Taccavi for new settlements — continuity of the instrument across different sultans

concepts.name: Capital Transfer to Daulatabad: Fiscal and Revenue Dimensions
key_dimensions: Revenue motive: access to Deccan's wealth and reducing the cost of southern campaigns — not purely administrative
Disruption to Delhi's revenue hinterland and trade networks — economic cost often underplayed
Failure: northern revenue base (Doab, Punjab) could not be effectively administered from Daulatabad — span-of-control problem
Reversal and double cost: re-transfer equally disruptive — fiscal lesson on infrastructure-revenue interdependence

concepts.name: Banjaras and Internal Trade Taxation: Non-Agricultural Revenue
key_dimensions: Banjaras as grain traders/transporters critical to Alauddin's market control system — their regulation as indirect revenue tool
Transit duties (Rahdari) on goods movement — a significant non-agricultural revenue source across the Sultanate period
Alauddin's control of Banjaras to ensure grain supply to Delhi markets — market intervention with revenue and military logic
Distinction between Rahdari (transit tax) and Zakat on trade goods — two parallel levies on commerce, often confused

concepts.name: Waqf and Religious Endowments: Interaction with State Revenue
key_dimensions: Waqf lands as revenue-exempt religious endowments — reducing the taxable land base, especially under Firuz Shah's generous grants
Firuz Shah's extensive Waqf grants to mosques, madrasas, and dargahs — fiscal cost of religious patronage
Tension between Sharia obligation to respect Waqf and state need to maximize Kharaj revenue — a structural fiscal dilemma
Contrast: Alauddin subordinating religious considerations to state revenue needs vs. Firuz's theocratic fiscal approach

concepts.name: Salary vs. Revenue Assignment: Cash Payment Experiments of Alauddin Khalji
key_dimensions: Alauddin's shift from Iqta assignments to direct cash salaries for soldiers — radical centralization of military finance
Feasibility linked to market control reforms keeping prices low — systemic interdependence of policies
Diwan-i-Ariz (military pay department) role in administering cash payments — institutional innovation
Post-Alauddin collapse: why cash salary system was abandoned by successors — sustainability and institutional capacity questions

concepts.name: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's Revenue Moderation Policy: Principles of Gradualism
key_dimensions: Reversal of Muhammad bin Tughlaq's (as prince Jauna Khan's) harsh revenue experiments — father-son policy contrast
Principle: revenue increase should be gradual (1/10th or 1/11th per year) to avoid agrarian disruption — an early articulation of sustainable taxation
Balancing treasury needs with peasant capacity — moderate statecraft as a UPSC values-based question angle
His policy as a model later echoed by Sher Shah and Akbar — continuity of agrarian revenue principles across medieval period
